commit 4fd52c0e2ac60bfe643704ed3f15144b4de6f835
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-10 19:50:48 +0530

    docs: make the rtk setup copy-pasteable, and fix three stale README claims
    
    The "Running alongside rtk" section described the two sane setups but left the
    reader to work out the JSON. It now shows both: a one-line diff for replacing
    rtk's hook, and the full settings.json plus the defer_to_rtk line for running
    both. It also says plainly that the one combination to avoid is adding the
    second hook *without* defer_to_rtk, and that one-at-a-time is the setup to use
    when evaluating toktrim, since with both hooks running you cannot tell which
    tool produced any given output.
    
    Three claims in the v0.3.1 README were still describing v0.3.0 behaviour. The
    replacements for them silently failed to apply in that commit because the text
    I matched against differed in line wrapping, and nothing checked:
    
    - the opening still called toktrim "a fallback output filter ... meant to sit
      alongside rtk", when it is standalone;
    - a known limitation still said what the hook skips "depends on whether rtk is
      installed";
    - another still explained the race as the reason "toktrim skips everything rtk
      handles", which is no longer how it works.
    
    Two bugs in the hook debugging examples, both of which would have misled anyone
    following them:
    
    - `git status` was annotated "(nothing — rtk's territory)". Standalone, it is
      wrapped.
    - `TOKTRIM_HOOK_DEBUG=1 echo '...' | toktrim hook` sets the variable on echo,
      not on toktrim, so it printed nothing and looked broken. The variable now goes
      on toktrim, with a note about why.
    
    Every example in the hook section was run against the built binary and produces
    exactly what is documented. Checked too: all JSON snippets parse, code fences
    balance, internal anchors resolve, and no stale claim from v0.2 or v0.3.0
    survives.

commit 0e5b7f6fb501b06c1b7223a4fccf93051ecc0003

    v0.3.1: standalone by default, not rtk-dependent

commit b0a26a669a79c7f414906911cbba9c0c7a21cf30
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-10 19:34:33 +0530

    fix: make toktrim standalone by default instead of rtk-dependent
    
    The hook deferred to rtk whenever the rtk *binary* was on PATH. That was wrong
    on two counts, and it made toktrim unusable as a tool in its own right.
    
    Wrong signal. Binary presence says nothing about whether rtk's hook is running.
    Someone who kept rtk installed but disabled its hook got the worst of both:
    toktrim stood down on git, jest and cargo, and rtk was not there to take them,
    so nothing filtered them at all.
    
    Wrong default. The deference came from the v0.2 issue framing toktrim as "a
    fallback filter for commands rtk doesn't handle", and the skip list was built
    from that issue's description of rtk's coverage. Measured against rtk 0.44.2,
    that description is well out of date: rtk claims about seventy commands,
    including npm run, docker, dotnet, go and make. Six of twenty common commands
    were claimed by both hooks, and since both answer with updatedInput and Claude
    Code takes whichever finishes last, which tool filtered a command was
    non-deterministic.
    
    toktrim does not need rtk. Its own test-runner filter already covers jest,
    vitest, mocha, node:test, pytest, go test and cargo. So the default is now
    standalone: toktrim handles everything it understands, and its remaining skip
    rules -- long-running or interactive commands, queries, redirects,
    self-selecting pipelines -- are its own judgement rather than a map of another
    tool.
    
    Deference is opt-in, via defer_to_rtk in toktrim.toml or
    TOKTRIM_DEFER_TO_RTK=1, for people who run both hooks. When on, toktrim asks
    rtk's own hook whether it claims the command instead of consulting a copy of
    its allowlist. That is accurate for whatever rtk is installed, answers the
    question that actually matters, and costs about 10 ms. A chain is deferred only
    when rtk claims every segment, because rtk will not rewrite a mixed chain and
    deferring would leave it unfiltered. Any failure to ask means toktrim handles
    the command: deference must never be the reason nothing filters it.
    
    Acceptance test 8 is now asserted in the condition it describes -- deference on,
    rtk claiming the command -- with a companion test pinning the standalone
    default. rtk's answer is stubbed in tests rather than invoked, so they do not
    change meaning when rtk is upgraded.
    
    README gains a "Running alongside rtk" section explaining the race and the two
    sane configurations, and no longer describes toktrim as a fallback.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

    test: cover the failure-block rules directly
    
    Three cases the fixtures exercise only indirectly:
    
    - a mocha-shaped block whose diff body sits at the same indentation as the
      AssertionError above it, asserting every diff line is both kept and marked
      as failure detail, that the summary closes the block rather than being
      swallowed, and that context reaches exactly three lines back;
    - a block past MaxBlockLines, asserting the marker is emitted and lands at the

      of swallowing the rest of the output.

    called a line one row above the failure 'two lines above' and expected it to be
    unprotected, when a three-line context window is supposed to cover it.

commit 681f17b90b387c4eca83f4beadad2a7792bc5a99
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-10 18:28:54 +0530

    test: pin rtk presence instead of inheriting it from the machine
    
    CI failed on both runners with "AT8: git status should print nothing", and the
    failure was real rather than flaky.
    
    Acceptance test 8 and v0.3 item 5 pull in opposite directions. AT8 says
    `git status` must print nothing because it is rtk's territory; item 5 says that
    when rtk is *not* installed toktrim should handle those commands, since
    otherwise nothing filters them. Both cannot hold on the same machine, and which
    one applies depends on whether rtk is on PATH. The GitHub runners have no rtk;
    the machine this was developed on does, which is why the suite passed locally
    and failed in CI.
    
    The tests now pin the condition instead of inheriting it. hook.RunWith takes an
    explicit Classifier so the unit tests choose whether rtk counts as present, and
    the binary-level tests put a fake rtk on PATH for the with-rtk case and an empty
    PATH for the without. Both behaviours are asserted, so neither requirement is
    quietly dropped:
    
      with rtk     git status -> skipped   (acceptance test 8)
      without rtk  git status -> wrapped   (v0.3 item 5)
    
    Verified by running the suite with rtk removed from PATH, which reproduces the
    CI environment. The README's known limitations now state plainly that what the
    hook skips depends on whether rtk is installed, and that the same command can
    be wrapped on one machine and skipped on another.
    
    Also adds the exhaustive mocha assertions the spec asks for: every +/- diff
    line, counted, and every file:line reference must survive, rather than a
    sample. A spot check of the expected value alone would have passed v0.2.0,
    which kept 6 of 6 `+  "total": 120` lines and 3 of 6 `-  "total": 118` lines.
    A companion check confirms the exhaustive version does report the captured
    v0.2.0 output as broken.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 3b96d88a708c209dc11d3fe4f35b9e6c95f18bd9
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-10 18:22:20 +0530

    feat: record what each run saved, and add toktrim stats
    
    Item 7 of the v0.3 spec, plus the documentation and floors the acceptance
    criteria ask for.
    
    Every `run` and `pipe` appends one JSON object to the ledger: timestamp,
    command (first 80 bytes, cut on a rune boundary), the filters that actually
    fired, raw bytes, output bytes, exit code and the raw log path if one was kept.
    It lives in $XDG_STATE_HOME/toktrim or ~/.local/state/toktrim on Unix and
    %LOCALAPPDATA%\toktrim on Windows, overridable with TOKTRIM_STATE_DIR and
    switchable off with TOKTRIM_NO_LEDGER=1.
    
    Every write is best effort and silent. A ledger is a convenience and must never
    be the reason a command behaves differently, so a missing directory, an
    unwritable file and a marshalling error are all swallowed. Each entry is written
    in one syscall so that concurrent toktrim runs append whole lines rather than
    interleaving halves, and Read skips a malformed line rather than failing, since
    a half-written line should not hide the rest.
    
    `toktrim stats [--since 7d]` reports totals, the token estimate (bytes/4,
    labelled as an estimate) and the top commands by bytes saved. Runs are grouped
    by command, looking *through* a shell wrapper: the hook wraps everything as
    `bash -c '<original>'`, so without that every row would read "bash" and the
    report would say nothing. `--since` takes 7d, 2w, 12h or 30m, and a bare `7d`
    works as shorthand.
    
    Stats also prunes raw logs older than raw_log_max_age_days (7 by default,
    configurable, 0 to disable). The runs that create those logs never clean them
    up -- deleting one would defeat the footer that names it -- and stats is the
    command someone runs when they are thinking about them anyway.
    
    Found while wiring this up: the test suite was writing real ledger entries into
    the developer's own ~/.local/state/toktrim, because the acceptance tests invoke
    the built binary. Every such invocation now gets TOKTRIM_NO_LEDGER=1 and
    test-owned state and raw-log directories, and a check confirms the suite leaves
    the real path untouched.
    
    Documentation and floors:
    
    - TestMeasuredSavings now covers all thirteen fixtures, with the floors raised
      to what the code actually achieves and per-fixture assertions naming the
      strings that must survive -- including `-  "total": 118`, the line v0.2.0
      dropped.
    - README: the measured table gains rows for all six new fixtures; the three 0%
      rows are explained rather than hidden, since each is a deliberate outcome.
      "What it deliberately skips" documents queries, self-selecting pipelines and
      the rtk-only-when-installed rule. Two new guarantees are stated (a failure
      block is kept whole; filtering never grows the output) and five new known
      limitations, including that `toktrim pipe` cannot tell a query from a build
      because classification needs the command line.
    - toktrim.example.toml documents similar_window and raw_log_max_age_days.
    
    Still no dependencies, still builds with GOPROXY=off, and all five release
    targets cross-compile.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit cb6ca18b714edc9cae55b9fe4fc112f24da97cfb
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-09 00:41:27 +0530

    fix: never emit more output than came in
    
    Item 6 of the v0.3 spec. On eslint output where every line is an error,
    v0.2.0's output was 2.89% larger than its input: nothing could be dropped, so
    the only thing the filters contributed was markers.
    
    Two fixes, at different levels.
    
    The direct cause was in Truncate. When every line evicted from the tail window
    was protected, it still printed "... output elided; failures from the middle
    follow ..." and "... resuming at the last N lines ...", even though it had
    dropped nothing -- claiming information had been removed when none had, and
    growing the output to say so. With skipped == 0 it now emits the held lines and
    the tail with no markers at all, which reconstructs the stream exactly. That
    alone takes the eslint fixture from +2.89% to +0.00%.
    
    The general guarantee is in the Processor. While the output still fits in the
    decision window (1 MiB) it holds both the raw bytes and the chain's output, and
    at Close emits whichever is smaller -- footer included in the comparison. If the
    raw form wins, the log is deleted too: there is nothing to recover when nothing
    was removed. Past the window toktrim commits to the filtered form and streams
    it, since a command producing megabytes is not one where markers could outweigh
    what was removed, and holding more would risk losing buffered output if toktrim
    itself were killed.
    
    Adding the window surfaced a bug in its own right, now covered by a test: the
    bytes buffered before the passthrough thresholds were crossed were fed to the
    filter chain but never written to the raw log, so the log was missing the start
    of the output. The log and the chain now advance off a single offset, which is
    what makes it impossible for them to disagree.
    
    Measured across the fixtures, no output is larger than its input:
      eslint-all-errors    8106 ->   8106  +0.00%
      dotnet-build-error   1827 ->   1827  +0.00%
      mocha-multi-fail    52301 ->   4684 -91.04%
      npm-install        186289 ->   7124 -96.18%
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit c848802b88892b82e0cab9741a25b5caee8e0f9e
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-09 00:32:38 +0530

    feat: leave query commands alone, and only defer to rtk when rtk is installed
    
    Items 4 and 5 of the v0.3 spec.
    
    4. A query's output is the answer, so it is never truncated.
    
    `npm ls --all` on a five-dependency project is 3145 lines, and v0.2.0 cut it to
    435 -- losing the middle third, which is where most of the tree lives. In the
    captured fixture math-intrinsics, axobject-query, shebang-regex and
    terminal-link all appear only between lines 1048 and 2096, and all four were
    gone. Looking a package up is the entire reason to run the command.
    
    Both halves of the spec's suggestion are implemented, since they cover
    different entry points. The hook now skips queries outright: npm/pnpm/yarn
    ls/outdated/view/why/info/explain/search/audit, gh, cat, jq, head, non-follow
    tail, `sed -n`, awk, `git config/remote/rev-parse/describe`, and any pipeline
    whose last stage is head, tail, grep, wc, sort, uniq, cut or jq -- whoever wrote
    that pipeline already chose how much output they wanted. And `toktrim run` run
    by hand on a query gets a chain with no truncation filter, so the protection
    holds even when the hook is not involved.
    
    Dedup's cross-gap window is also switched off for queries. In a dependency tree
    or a config dump the same line at a different position is still information; it
    was quietly removing 349 lines from the npm ls fixture. With that off, the
    fixture now passes through byte-identical, which is the honest answer: there is
    nothing in a dependency tree that can be dropped safely.
    
    5. rtk's allowlist only applies when rtk is on PATH.
    
    jest, vitest, pytest, tsc, eslint, cargo, go test and git status/log/diff/show
    were skipped unconditionally, so on a machine without rtk nothing filtered them
    at all -- even though toktrim's own test-runner filter already understands jest,
    pytest, go test and cargo. The hook now looks rtk up once per process and only
    defers when it is really there.
    
    Binary runners are normalised before the skip list is consulted, which fixes
    the inconsistency where `npx jest` was wrapped while bare `jest` was skipped.
    npx, bunx, pnpx, `pnpm exec` and `yarn dlx` are unwrapped unconditionally.
    `yarn <x>` is unwrapped only when x is a recognised tool, because `yarn jest`
    runs a binary while `yarn build` runs a package script, and `npm run x` is
    never unwrapped for the same reason.
    
    Tests cover both rtk states, including one that writes a fake rtk into a
    temporary PATH to exercise the lookup itself rather than the injected flag.
    Verified against the built binary: with rtk present, `jest`, `npx jest` and
    `tsc` are skipped; with PATH stripped, all three are wrapped, while queries,
    long-running commands and self-selecting pipelines stay skipped either way.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 62c9c0a6916a2f4a4abd75af7f6ccdbaf2e6e70b
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-10-09 00:27:03 +0530

    fix: keep failure blocks whole, detect mocha/TAP, collapse near-identical noise
    
    Items 1-3 of the v0.3 spec.
    
    1. Failure blocks were being partially dropped (the reported bug).
    
    A mocha run of 400 passing tests and 6 failures fell through to the generic
    truncate filter. Inside the rescued failures, `+  "total": 120` survived and
    `-  "total": 118` did not, along with the six `field_*` lines, and no marker was
    left behind -- so the diff read as complete while saying something false.
    
    The cause was that a failure was only ever protected by a fixed ±3-line context
    window. `+  "total": 120` happened to fall inside the window of the
    `at Context.<anonymous>` frame below it; `-  "total": 118` was one line further
    out. A context window is simply the wrong tool here: an assertion diff is as
    long as it needs to be, and keeping its edges while dropping its middle is the
    worst available outcome.
    
    Guard now understands failure *blocks*. A line that opens one -- a mocha
    numbered failure, a jest ●, a traceback, an AssertionError, a TAP `not ok` --
    puts it into block mode, where every line is protected until the block closes
    on a sibling header, a summary line, or a dedent. Deciding continuation needs
    both indentation and shape, because mocha prints `+ expected - actual` and the
    diff body at the same indentation as the AssertionError above it. A block over
    DefaultMaxBlockLines (500) is cut with a marker at the point of the cut; nothing
    inside a failure is ever dropped silently.
    
    All six blocks in the fixture now come out byte-for-byte identical.
    
    2. mocha, node:test and TAP are now detected.
    
    jsTestMarker only matched jest and vitest, so mocha never reached the test
    filter. Added `N passing/failing/pending`, `ok N`, `not ok N`, `# tests N` and
    `TAP version N`, and taught testPassLine and testBlockEnd the ✔ glyph that
    mocha has defaulted to since v8 -- only ✓ and √ were there. Everything after
    mocha's `N failing` line is treated as failure detail. A dropped TAP result also
    takes its indented YAML diagnostic with it, which otherwise left orphaned
    `---` / `duration_ms:` / `...` fragments behind.
    
    3. Dedup now collapses near-identical lines, carefully.
    
    Two rules: an adjacent run collapses to its first line plus a marker where the
    run ended; a line repeating an earlier one across a gap is dropped once that
    shape has already appeared a few times, totalled once at the end.
    
    Both compare by *shape* -- numbers, ids, hashes, timestamps and quoted values
    blanked -- but only for lines that announce themselves as logging. That
    restriction is not cosmetic. Blanket shape matching collapsed `unique line 0`
    through `unique line 49` into one line in an existing test, and would have done
    the same to `[  1/400] CC module_001.o`: there the number *is* the content.
    Restricting it to log-shaped lines gets the compression without that risk, and
    a test now pins both halves.
    
    The cross-gap rule exists because an application log alternates shapes -- db
    line, http line, db line -- so its repeats are never adjacent and the run rule
    alone never fires. Runs of blank lines also collapse to one, since dropping
    interleaved content otherwise leaves a stack of separators.
    
    New invariant tests over every fixture: every failure line in the input reaches
    the output in order; no line inside a failure block is missing without a marker
    at that position; and no fixture's output is larger than its input.
    TestInvariantCatchesTheV020Bug runs the gap invariant against output captured
    from the released v0.2.0 binary and asserts it still reports the three
    truncated blocks, so the invariant cannot quietly become a tautology -- the
    first two versions of that test passed only because they called the production
    block detector, or because another layer happened to protect the blocks.
    
    Measured on the fixtures:
      mocha-multi-fail   967 -> 152 lines, all 6 blocks byte-identical
      node-test-tap      120 ->  28 lines, failing diagnostic intact
      mocha-pass         221 ->  54 lines, all 12 suite names kept
      node-app-logs      154 ->  20 lines, 11761 -> 1311 bytes (88.8%)
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 210db7c608d68a781c28afb0c35995c4e4b3c06d
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-09-30 00:05:23 +0530

    feat: add releases, CI on windows and linux, and a version command
    
    Phase 4 of the rtk-fallback spec.
    
    Distribution: a goreleaser config building linux, darwin and windows for amd64
    and arm64 (windows/arm64 excluded), with sha256 checksums. Two archive sets, so
    a Windows user can download toktrim_windows_amd64.exe directly rather than
    unpacking something first, while the tar.gz/zip archives carry the licence,
    readme and example config. Binaries are CGO_ENABLED=0 and -trimpath.
    
    `toktrim version` reports version, commit, build date, Go version and platform.
    goreleaser injects them with -ldflags; a binary built by `go install` has none of
    those, so version falls back to the module version and VCS stamps the toolchain
    embeds rather than reporting "dev".
    
    CI on ubuntu-latest and windows-latest: go vet, gofmt, go build, go test -race,
    the golden tests, the hook JSON tests and the acceptance tests each called out
    separately, plus a check that the goldens are not stale. Two further jobs: one
    asserting go.mod has no requirements and that the tree builds with GOPROXY=off,
    since toktrim must work with the network disabled; one running goreleaser check
    and a snapshot build that asserts the Windows .exe is among the release
    artifacts. A release only publishes after its tests pass.
    
    Cross-compiling for the release found a bug that a macOS-only build could not:
    syscall.SIGBREAK does not exist on Windows, so internal/runner did not compile
    for the hook's main target. The Go runtime's console control handler maps both
    CTRL_C_EVENT and CTRL_BREAK_EVENT onto SIGINT, so os.Interrupt is what a Ctrl-C
    and a Ctrl-Break both arrive as; listening for it covers the spec's requirement.
    This is exactly what the windows-latest CI job is for.
    
    TestMeasuredSavings pins the compression figures quoted in the README to the
    recorded fixtures as floors, so a documentation claim cannot drift from what the
    code does, and asserts per fixture which strings must survive. The old "70-95%"
    claim is gone, replaced by measured numbers with the fixture that produced each.
    One of them is 0%: a failing jest run is almost entirely failure information, so
    toktrim leaves it alone. TestFixturesHaveProvenance keeps every fixture
    accountable for where it came from.
    
    README rewritten: what toktrim does, what it deliberately skips and why,
    install from Releases, the hook snippet, the full config reference, the five
    guarantees, and seven known limitations -- including that two PreToolUse hooks
    returning updatedInput for one command race, which is the real reason the skip
    list matters when running alongside rtk.
    
    PROJECT_SUMMARY.md and BUILD_INSTRUCTIONS.md are removed. Both still advertised
    tiktoken, the placeholder module path and the 70-95% figure; their useful
    content (install, build, development, CI) is in the README.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit cb2d7d4b8c8e9b7e7894295277474fd464319ccd
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-09-29 23:58:12 +0530

    feat: add the Claude Code PreToolUse hook
    
    Phase 3 of the rtk-fallback spec.
    
    `toktrim hook` reads a PreToolUse payload from stdin and, for a Bash command it
    wants to handle, prints hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput.command wrapping it as
    
        toktrim run -- bash -c '<original>'
    
    with each ' escaped as '\''. Going through bash keeps pipes, &&, redirects and
    quoting working; only the final output is filtered. Otherwise it prints nothing
    and exits 0.
    
    On permissionDecision, as the spec asked. The hook never returns one. Claude
    Code's hooks reference documents exit 0 with no decision as "the hook has no
    decision to report, so the tool call continues through the normal permission
    flow", and lists permissionDecision and updatedInput as independent fields of
    hookSpecificOutput. Returning updatedInput alone therefore rewrites the command
    and leaves the permission prompt exactly where it was, which is the behaviour
    we want: toktrim wraps arbitrary commands and must never be the reason one skips
    the user's prompt. The docs' own example pairs updatedInput with "allow", but
    nothing requires that pairing, and a test asserts the field is absent from every
    reply. Documented in the README, including the caveat that the docs do not spell
    out this exact combination.
    
    The same reference turned up something worth knowing for anyone running toktrim
    next to rtk: when two PreToolUse hooks both return updatedInput for one tool
    call, the one that finishes last wins, and hooks run in parallel. So the skip
    list is not only about compression -- it is what stops the two hooks racing over
    the same command. It is in the README as a known limitation.
    
    Left alone: anything starting with rtk or toktrim; everything rtk's allowlist
    covers (git status/log/diff/show, cargo, go test, pytest, jest, vitest, tsc,
    eslint, ls, grep, find); long-running or interactive commands (dev, start,
    watch, serve, --watch, -it, tail -f, docker run without --rm); and commands
    already sending all output to a file. Chains are handled, since rtk does not
    rewrite them -- unless every segment is itself an rtk command.
    
    Two details worth noting: `go build` is wrapped although `go test` is not,
    because rtk's allowlist covers only the latter, and the same applies to git
    subcommands beyond status/log/diff/show. Leading VAR=value assignments are
    skipped when finding the command name, so `NODE_ENV=production npm run dev` is
    still recognised as long-running.
    
    Every error path is silent and lets the command through unchanged; the hook
    returns 0 unconditionally. TOKTRIM_HOOK_DEBUG=1 explains why it stayed quiet.
    
    Acceptance tests 8, 9, 10 and 11 are automated, both against the package and
    end to end through the built binary.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 405d3ac3c2b960bb70d8e6089fcde7f0cf72d038
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-09-29 23:52:58 +0530

    feat: add filters for the commands rtk skips
    
    Phase 2 of the rtk-fallback spec. Every filter has a recorded fixture under
    testdata/ and a golden test (`go test ./internal/golden -update` regenerates).
    
    Filters, in chain order:
    
    - ansi: strips CSI/OSC escapes, reduces a line redrawn with \r to the text left
      on screen, and collapses a run of progress readouts to the last one, so a
      download bar becomes one line showing its final state.
    - node-install: drops deprecation warnings, registry/arborist chatter and
      funding notices; keeps ERR! blocks and the "added N packages" summary.
    - test-runner: block aware. Once a failure block opens, every line is kept
      until the next suite header, so a failing test's name, assertion and stack
      frames survive even when they run past Guard's context window. For
      `npm run <script>` it stays a pass-through until the output identifies itself
      as jest or vitest, since a script may be anything.
    - docker-build: buffers each BuildKit step until it reports a status, because
      whether a step's output matters is only known once it finishes. A successful
      step collapses to a count; a failing step is replayed in full.
    - dotnet: collapses per-project restore and build lines; keeps diagnostics with
      their codes and the build/test summary.
    - dedup, then truncate: the generic backstop. Truncation keeps the first 30 and
      last 60 lines plus any failure line in between, tracked by position so order
      is preserved rather than reordered into a trailing block.
    
    Two fixes the fixtures forced out, neither of which unit tests had caught:
    
    - npm renamed "npm WARN" to "npm warn" in v11, so the case-sensitive patterns
      matched nothing. All 17 deprecation warnings in the recorded install were
      passing through.
    - Package names are full of failure words -- error-ex, makeerror, es-errors,
      json-parse-even-better-errors -- so every line of npm's registry chatter
      looked like a failure, was protected, and dragged three lines of context in
      with it. Failure detection now ignores tokens containing a URL scheme.
      The recorded install went from 160 lines to 22.
    
    Guard also now separates "must keep" from "worth showing context for". A
    compiler diagnostic names its own file, line and code, so surrounding it with
    three lines of restore chatter added noise; a panic or traceback still gets its
    neighbours.
    
    Measured on the recorded fixtures:
      npm install      1871 -> 22 lines,  186289 -> 867 bytes   (99.5%)
      docker build       84 -> 52 lines, failing step intact
      dotnet build       23 -> 17 lines, all diagnostics intact
      jest (failing)     45 -> 32 lines, every failure intact
      make (400 lines)  406 -> 102 lines, middle failures rescued
    
    Config: toktrim.toml in the project root or ~/.config/toktrim/, with per-filter
    switches and adjustable limits. Parsed by a small TOML-subset reader rather than
    a dependency, keeping the module dependency-free; unknown keys and unsupported
    value types are reported instead of ignored. A malformed config is never fatal.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 5a7960b5da819e08f6bef15e259fdf18cdf8c25a
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-09-29 23:37:22 +0530

    feat: stream output through a line pipeline instead of buffering it
    
    Phase 1 of the rtk-fallback spec.
    
    Output is now processed line by line as it arrives. Previously the whole
    output was held in memory until the command exited, so anything killed by
    Claude Code's two-minute Bash timeout produced nothing at all.
    
    Architecture:
    
    - filter.LineFilter replaces the old string-in/string-out Filter. The pipeline
      pushes one Line at a time and the filter pushes zero or more lines onward.
      Filters that need a whole block may buffer that block; none may buffer the
      whole stream.
    - filter.Guard runs at the head of every chain and marks lines carrying failure
      information, plus three lines of context on each side, as Protected. No later
      filter may drop or rewrite a protected line. Protecting context *before* a
      failure means holding that many lines back, so Guard delays the stream by
      three lines and never drops anything.
    - pipeline.Processor is an io.Writer, so the runner copies the child's output
      straight into it. It holds raw bytes until the output passes 40 lines or
      2 KB; if the command ends first, those exact bytes are written out, so small
      output is byte-for-byte identical. Past the threshold it starts filtering and
      tees the raw stream to a temp file, and the filtered output ends with
      "[toktrim] N lines elided — full output: <path>". If nothing was actually
      trimmed the log is removed again and no footer is added.
    - Dedup is now a streaming run-length encoder holding a single line back, so
      memory does not grow with the length of a run.
    
    Signals: SIGINT/SIGTERM (and Ctrl-Break on Windows) are relayed to the child
    and everything processed so far is flushed. Windows cannot deliver a signal to
    another process, so the relay kills the child there, which is documented.
    
    Tests cover the guarantees rather than the implementation: small output is
    identical for every chunk boundary from 1 byte upward, filter output does not
    depend on how the stream was chunked, failure lines and stack frames survive
    compression, and the raw log holds the complete output.
    
    Acceptance tests 1, 5, 6, 7 and 11 are automated in cmd/toktrim/main_test.go.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 3a9ac380362dafead6009a0d95863090e80c97e9
Author: dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   2026-09-29 23:30:09 +0530

    fix: correct exit-code ordering, merge output streams, drop network dependency
    
    Phase 0 of the rtk-fallback spec: make the existing tool behave correctly
    before building anything new on top of it.
    
    - Rename the module to github.com/dev/toktrim so that
      `go install github.com/dev/toktrim/cmd/toktrim@latest` resolves.
    - ExecuteCommand printed nothing for failing commands: os.Exit ran inside the
      Cmd.Wait error branch, before the filtered output was written. Output (and
      optional stats) is now written first and the child's exit code is propagated
      afterwards. A command that cannot be started exits 127.
    - Give the child a single os.Pipe for both stdout and stderr so the two stay
      in the order the child wrote them, instead of concatenating two buffers
      after the fact.
    - Replace tiktoken-go with an offline chars/4 estimate. toktrim must work with
      the network disabled, and tiktoken downloads its vocabulary from OpenAI on
      first use. The dollar figure is gone; the count is labelled an estimate.
    - Gate stats behind TOKTRIM_STATS=1. Claude Code forwards the Bash tool's
      stderr to the model, so unconditional telemetry costs the tokens it claims
      to save.
    - Fix a trailing-newline bug shared by all three filters: splitting on "\n"
      yields a final empty element that was emitted as a stray blank line, so
      every filtered output gained a blank line. Add splitLines/joinLines.
    - Add `run` as the primary subcommand name (`exec` stays as an alias).
    - Drop the README's approver/validator hook snippet. Neither field exists in
      Claude Code.
    
    The dedup and diff test expectations were self-contradictory (the dedup case
    expected both a "[Repeated 3 times]" summary and the three original lines, so
    no implementation could pass) and had been failing since they were added in
    44ab9bb. They now assert the documented behaviour.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
